extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in computational humor and multimodal NLP (e.g., people building/evaluating caption-contest models and datasets)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures, annotation guidelines, dataset construction rules, and evaluation metrics for modeling, ranking, matching, and explaining captions in The New Yorker cartoon caption contest; aimed at building/assessing models that predict relevance, funniness, and produce human-like explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-performing features for identifying funniest captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Features empirically found to perform best for identifying the funniest caption among a set: perplexity, match to image setting and uncanniness description, readability, proper nouns, overlap with WordNet's “person” and “relative” synsets, lexical centrality among submissions, and sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features were identified in prior work (Shahaf et al., Radev et al.) and form direct analogs to the paper's own “location” and “uncanny description” annotations; use these features (and similar annotations) when building models to detect the funniest caption.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-quality caption identification
rubrics_metrics.description: For each contest, construct a set of high-quality captions by: (a) automatically adding official New Yorker finalists if available; (b) otherwise considering the top-5 crowd-ranked captions (from Jain et al., 2020) and selecting 3 diverse candidates via semantic deduplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When official finalists are available include them; when using crowd ratings discard duplicates, then apply embedding-based semantic deduplication (SBERT vectors, hierarchical clustering) and sample one candidate per cluster to ensure diversity. Final high-quality sets total 2.7K captions across 704 contests in this study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic deduplication for diverse candidate selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use SBERT (paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2) to compute vectors for candidate captions, perform hierarchical clustering, and sample a single candidate from each cluster to produce a representative and diverse set of high-quality captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces near-duplicate captions among the selected high-quality candidates; implement clustering on the SBERT embeddings and choose one per cluster to maintain diversity among finalists used to construct instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching-instance construction (negative sampling rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a matching instance for each high-quality caption as the correct answer; form negative (mismatched) options by randomly assigning captions to other contests subject to constraints: assignments occur only within cross-validation splits; construct negatives so each answer appears exactly once as the correct answer and exactly four times as an incorrect option elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constraints avoid train/test leakage and prevent 'answer-only' biases in the corpus. Ensure random assignment respects cross-validation split boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality-ranking-instance construction (sampling 'okay' negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: To build quality-ranking instances, sample 'okay' captions (near-misses) from the contest's submissions: when crowd ratings exist, discard the top and bottom third and sample from the middle tertile; when ratings are unavailable, train a text-only quality-ranking model on crowd-labelled data to estimate quality and sample accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also deduplicate exact string matches so 'okay' captions aren't exact copies of high-quality captions or of each other. For older contests without ratings, the authors trained a quality-ranking model on 253 contests and used top/bottom-1000-per-contest samples to create good/bad corpora (≈506K captions) to support sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for answer-only bias in corpus construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming instances, ensure negative assignments are made such that there is no answer-only bias: every answer appears exactly once as correct and exactly four times as incorrect in other instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit bookkeeping in negative sampling prevents artifacts where certain captions are recognizable as always-correct/always-incorrect due to dataset construction rather than model understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation types and sampling frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect four annotation types per cartoon: locations, natural-language descriptions, 'uncanny' descriptions (what's unusual), and entity/Wikipedia links. In this study: Cartoon description HITs were run 3× per cartoon, Wikipedia-links HITs 2× per cartoon, and pairwise explanations HITs were run many times (e.g., 2.7K HITs overall) to support pairwise comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At test time select a single randomly sampled valid tuple of annotations (held constant across methods). During training, use all available annotation variants. Keep annotation multiplicity in mind when building models that condition on human-written ancillary information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tuple construction preserving annotator-level dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Because some annotation types were collected within the same HIT (e.g., descriptions and uncanny descriptions; locations and entity links), construct tuples at the annotator level to preserve within-annotator dependencies. Concretely, consider the six valid tuples holding author constant (3(description,uncanny) × 2(location,link)) and sample one valid tuple per cartoon for evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids invalid combinations where an ‘uncanny description’ references entities introduced only in some other annotator's description; keep author-constancy when combining annotation types into single inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical Turk worker qualification criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify crowdworkers for annotation tasks, require: residency from the set {AU, CA, NZ, GB, US}, at least 10,000 prior approved HITs, and a minimum acceptance rate of 97% on previous HITs. Qualification rounds involved manual grading of responses (e.g., 30 annotators graded in one round; 21 qualified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run specific qualification rounds per HIT type (description/link HITs separate from pairwise-explanation HITs); manually inspect and qualify annotators based on gold/seed items, and issue disclaimers for mature content as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairwise explanation judgment setup
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect pairwise judgments on explanations using a qualified pool of annotators: provide two explanations and ask which is better (or compare explanations against described desirable axes). The authors ran a second qualification round where annotators rated several manually selected 'good' and 'bad' joke explanations across desirable axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the qualification round to filter annotators for the pairwise-explanation tasks; only qualified annotators should participate in the final pairwise judgments to ensure quality comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation content standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A good explanation should explain how the joke/caption relates to the described situation and why it is funny (i.e., identify the mechanism by which the humor arises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation examples illustrate mapping elements of the scene to the wordplay/figurative meaning (e.g., points out puns, plays on idioms, incongruity resolution). Use this standard when collecting or grading explanations and when training/examining models to produce human-like explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for matching / ranking / explanation tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported task metrics include: CrowdAcc (↑) and NYAcc (↑) for matching/choice accuracy (higher is better); BLEU-4 (B-4, ↑) and Rouge-L (↑) and Perplexity (PPL, ↓) for explanation generation/quality-ranking (BLEU/ROUGE higher is better, PPL lower is better).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these standard automatic metrics alongside human (crowd and editor) accuracy estimates. Table 4 in the paper summarizes how different models scored on these metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-validation split constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct cross-validation splits so that training, validation, and testing captions are disjoint; only assign negative captions within cross-validation splits to prevent leakage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures fair evaluation: no caption used for training appears in validation or test instances. Maintain split-level isolation when sampling negatives and forming instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model fine-tuning / training procedures (reproducibility constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended/used training practices for models in the paper: validation-set early stopping on cross-entropy loss; fine-tune models separately per cross-validation split; select top-1 via beam search (n=5); use label-adjusted smoothed cross-entropy with smoothing=0.1; warmup / linear warmup steps (e.g., 200 steps) and small learning-rate searches per split; specified batch sizes (e.g., 32/64), image resizing/padding to 336px square, and image augmentations (random horizontal flip, color jitter, random grayscale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These hyperparameter and augmentation choices materially affect model performance (per reported experiments). When reproducing or comparing models, follow similar early stopping, smoothing, warmup, and data-augmentation settings and report them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy/IRB handling for crowd studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdworker IDs are hashed in public releases so annotations cannot be back-traced to individuals; the crowdworking studies were considered exempt under US federal regulation 45 CFR 46.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing crowd-annotated data, hash or anonymize worker identifiers and verify IRB/exemption requirements for non-sensitive tasks; provide content warnings for mature themes where necessary.
